The Atlantic white marlin (Kajikia albida) is a large, highly migratory istiophorid billfish that supports important recreational and commercial fisheries throughout the tropical and subtropical Atlantic Ocean. Field studies have documented that females achieve a maximum body length of 300 centimeters [Li = 300 centimeters], a size that is attained only after many years of growth in the productive pelagic environment these fish inhabit. This ultimate total length represents a substantial investment in somatic growth before the energetic demands of reproduction become a dominant feature of the life history. The species is characterized by rapid early growth, with individuals reaching approximately 164 centimeters [Lp = approximately 164 centimeters] in total length at the onset of sexual maturity, a size that corresponds to a body mass of about 40,264 grams [Wwp = about 40,264 grams] based on length-weight relationships derived from fisheries-dependent sampling. This pubertal length is notably smaller than the asymptotic size, indicating a prolonged period of adult growth during which individuals continue to increase in both body length and mass.

Reproductive output in Atlantic white marlin has been estimated from histological analysis of ovarian tissue collected from spawning females in the Gulf of Mexico and the western Caribbean Sea. At a water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], a mature female measuring around 179 centimeters in fork length produces on average 877,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 877,000 eggs per spawning event], and typically completes one spawning event per year [F_R_i = one spawning event per year], which reflects a high fecundity typical of pelagic spawners that release buoyant eggs into the ocean currents. The corresponding daily reproductive rate realized through multiple spawning events across an extended breeding season is approximately 2,403 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,403 eggs per day], though direct observation of individual spawning frequency remains challenging for this highly mobile species. This annual egg production is substantial even when compared to other large scombrids and istiophorids of similar body size, underscoring the reproductive potential of the species. The combination of high fecundity and protracted spawning allows Kajikia albida to exploit favorable oceanographic conditions for larval survival across a broad geographic range. The energetic cost of this reproductive output is significant and is reflected in the somatic growth patterns of adult females.

At the commencement of life, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva of Atlantic white marlin emerges from a pelagic egg measuring approximately 1.1 millimeters in diameter, which yields a newly hatched larva with a wet weight of only 0.0007 grams [Wwb = 0.0007 grams]. This minuscule birth mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy common among teleost pelagic spawners, wherein the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The larvae are planktonic and extremely vulnerable to predation and starvation during this early endotrophic phase. The duration of the yolk-sac stage is brief, as the larvae must quickly develop functional jaws and a digestive system to capture prey. Under the same thermal conditions of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the interval between fertilization and the hatching event is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], a rapid developmental pace that is characteristic of epipelagic fish larvae developing in warm surface waters. This short incubation period reduces the window of vulnerability for the developing embryo within the chorionated egg.

The wet weight at puberty of approximately 40,264 grams [Wwp = approximately 40,264 grams] represents a substantial increase from the sub-milligram hatchling mass, reflecting an extraordinary growth trajectory spanning several orders of magnitude during the juvenile and subadult phases. This pubertal body mass, which corresponds to a total length of 164 centimeters [Lp = 164 centimeters], is roughly fifteen percent of the ultimate wet weight achieved by the largest adults. The maximum adult wet weight in the species has been estimated at 268,210 grams [Wwi = 268,210 grams], based on the same length-weight power function applied to the asymptotic length of 300 centimeters [Li = 300 centimeters]. The substantial difference between mass at puberty and ultimate mass indicates that adult females continue to accumulate significant somatic tissue, a pattern that contrasts with smaller istiophorids where adult growth is more limited after maturity.

This maximum lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years] has been inferred from otolith increment analysis and tag-recapture studies, though validation of the oldest age classes remains an active area of research at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the age at hatching is consistently observed at 6 days after fertilization [ab = 6 days after fertilization], with the yolk-sac larva initiating exogenous feeding shortly thereafter. The combination of a short incubation period, high fecundity, and a moderately long adult lifespan positions the Atlantic white marlin as an iteroparous, K-selected species relative to smaller epipelagic teleosts, yet with a faster pace of life than the larger, longer-lived billfishes such as the swordfish (Xiphias gladius). These demographic traits have important implications for stock assessment and management.
